concept.name: Counting & Radix Sort

relationships.description: Connects Counting & Radix Sort to core algorithm patterns in the broader engineering catalog.

spark.summary: Counting and Radix Sort bypass the Ω(n log n) comparison lower bound by indexing keys directly into frequency buckets or sorting digit-by-digit in O(n + k) or O(d(n + b)) time.
spark.keyTakeaway: When keys are bounded integers, fixed-width strings, or IEEE-754 floats, non-comparative distribution sorting outperforms Quicksort and Timsort by eliminating branch mispredictions and log-factor passes.

concept.whyItMatters: Comparison sorts cannot beat Ω(n log n) comparisons in the decision-tree model, and random key comparisons trigger CPU branch mispredictions (~15–20 cycles per miss on modern x86_64 pipelines). In database query engines, columnar analytics (DuckDB, ClickHouse), GPU sorting (CUB/Thrust), and network packet schedulers, sorting millions of 32-bit or 64-bit keys using LSD/MSD Radix Sort cuts CPU cycles by 3x–8x and saturates memory bandwidth instead of stalling on conditional branches.
whenToUse: Sorting large arrays (n > 10,000) of fixed-width integers, timestamps, IPv4/IPv6 addresses, or IEEE-754 floats where key bit-width is small (32–128 bits).
Building high-throughput database operators (hash-join partitioning, columnar dictionary encoding, LSM-tree SSTable compaction) where branch-free throughput matters.
Sorting strings or byte-slices with shared prefixes using MSD Radix Sort (American Flag Sort) combined with insertion sort for small buckets (n <= 16).
whenNotToUse: Keys have a huge or unbounded value range k >> n (e.g., 64-bit UUIDs with pure Counting Sort), which blows up histogram memory to O(k).
Sorting small arrays (n < 64) where allocation and histogram-clearing overhead exceed O(n log n) comparison costs.
Ordering depends on arbitrary runtime comparators (locale-aware collation, multi-column dynamic SQL expressions) that cannot be mapped to lexicographic byte order.
keyPoints: Counting Sort runs in O(n + k) time and O(n + k) auxiliary space by computing a frequency histogram, taking a prefix sum for destination offsets, and scattering elements stably.
Radix Sort decomposes a w-bit key into d = ceil(w / r) digits of r bits each (typically r = 8 or r = 11, giving radix b = 256 or 2048) and runs Counting Sort per digit.

LSD (Least Significant Digit) Radix Sort processes digits right-to-left and requires each pass to be stable, whereas MSD (Most Significant Digit) recurses left-to-right and enables early termination on distinct prefixes.
Choosing radix r = 8 (256 buckets, 1 KB histogram in L1d cache) or r = 11 (2,048 buckets, 8 KB histogram in L1d cache) keeps the entire count array inside the 32–48 KB L1 data cache.

IEEE-754 floats and signed two's-complement integers can be radix-sorted without custom comparators using deterministic bit-flipping bijections (flipping the sign bit for signed ints; conditionally flipping all bits if negative for floats).

examples.title: Columnar OLAP Engine Sorting 100M 64-bit Event Timestamps
examples.scenario: A ClickHouse/DuckDB-style analytics query executes ORDER BY event_ts_ns LIMIT 100000000 on 100 million 8-byte nanosecond timestamps.
examples.outcome: An 8-pass LSD Radix Sort (8-bit radix, 256-entry L1-resident histogram) completes in ~420 ms on a single core with zero branch mispredictions, versus ~2.8 s for std::sort (Introsort), achieving a 6.6x speedup.

examples.title: In-Place MSD String Sorting with American Flag Sort
examples.scenario: A log ingestion service sorts 5 million URL paths (average length 48 bytes) before prefix compression and SSTable flushing.
examples.outcome: MSD Radix Sort partitions on byte 0, recurses only on non-trivial buckets, and switches to insertion sort below 16 elements, reducing memory overhead to O(alphabet + max_depth) and cutting L3 cache misses by 45%.

tradeOffs.pro: Larger r (e.g., r = 11 or 16) reduces the number of full-array passes d = ceil(w / r), cutting memory bandwidth traffic.
tradeOffs.con: Histogram size grows as 2^r (65,536 entries * 4 bytes = 256 KB for r = 16), spilling out of L1d cache (32–48 KB) into L2/L3 and stalling scatter writes.

tradeOffs.pro: LSD has completely predictable, non-recursive passes with uniform vectorizable loops and guaranteed stability.
tradeOffs.con: LSD always inspects every digit of every key even if keys diverge in the top byte, whereas MSD can short-circuit and run in-place.

tradeOffs.pro: Out-of-place ping-pong buffers (2 * n * sizeof(T)) allow sequential reads and clean prefix-sum scatters.
tradeOffs.con: Doubles peak RAM footprint compared to in-place American Flag Sort or Introsort, which matters when sorting multi-gigabyte buffers.

failureModes.name: Histogram L1 Cache Thrashing
failureModes.description: Picking a 16-bit radix (65,536 buckets = 256–512 KB) causes every scatter increment to miss L1d cache and hit L2/L3.
failureModes.mitigation: Cap radix at 8 bits (256 buckets, 1–2 KB) or 11 bits (2,048 buckets, 8–16 KB) so the entire histogram stays resident in L1d.

failureModes.name: Signed Integer & Float Sign-Bit Inversion
failureModes.description: Treating two's-complement negative integers or negative IEEE-754 floats as unsigned bit patterns places negative numbers after positive numbers (and reverses negative float order).
failureModes.mitigation: XOR the sign bit (key ^ (1 << (w - 1))) for signed integers; for IEEE-754 floats, flip all bits if sign bit is 1, else flip only the sign bit, then invert the transform after sorting.

failureModes.name: TLB & Cache-Line Aliasing on Scatter
failureModes.description: Writing to 256+ scattered bucket pointers in a single pass can exceed the CPU's L1 TLB entries (typically 64) or cause write-combining buffer thrashing.
failureModes.mitigation: Use small software write-combining buffers (e.g., 8–16 elements per bucket in L1) or keep radix to 8 bits with 4-KB page-aligned ping-pong buffers.

failureModes.name: Unbounded Key Range in Pure Counting Sort
failureModes.description: Running Counting Sort directly on sparse 32-bit IDs (k = 2^32) allocates 16 GB of zeroed count arrays and triggers OOM.
failureModes.mitigation: Never use single-pass Counting Sort when k > 4 * n; switch to multi-pass Radix Sort with bounded bucket size b = 256.

commonMistakes: Using unstable Counting Sort inside an LSD Radix Sort loop, which destroys the ordering established by lower-significance digits.
Forgetting to zero-initialize the histogram array between radix passes, corrupting prefix-sum offsets.
Allocating new output arrays inside every recursive call of MSD Radix Sort instead of reusing a single scratch buffer or sorting in-place.
Applying LSD Radix Sort to variable-length strings without right-padding shorter strings with a sentinel smaller than any valid character.
Benchmarking Radix Sort only on uniformly random integers and missing the fact that pre-sorted or nearly-sorted inputs still pay full d-pass bandwidth.

sections.content:
## The idea

Every comparison-based sorting algorithm—Quicksort, Mergesort, Heapsort, Timsort—models ordering as a binary decision tree. Because n! permutations require at least log2(n!) = Ω(n log n) binary decisions, no comparison sort can break that asymptotic barrier.

Counting Sort and Radix Sort sidestep comparisons entirely by exploiting the internal representation of keys. Counting Sort treats a key in [0, k) as a direct array index, tallying frequencies in a histogram, converting frequencies into starting write offsets via an exclusive prefix sum, and scattering elements into their final positions in O(n + k) time. Radix Sort generalizes this to large w-bit keys by slicing each key into d digits of r bits (base b = 2^r) and executing Counting Sort once per digit, achieving O(d(n + b)) time with zero key-to-key comparisons and zero data-dependent branches.

## Concrete walkthrough

Consider sorting 4 unsigned 16-bit integers [0x031A, 0x01FF, 0x0302, 0x0102] using 8-bit LSD Radix Sort (d = 2 passes, b = 256):

1. **Pass 0 (Low byte, shift = 0, mask = 0xFF)**:
   - Extract low bytes: 0x1A, 0xFF, 0x02, 0x02.
   - Histogram counts: count[0x02] = 2, count[0x1A] = 1, count[0xFF] = 1.
   - Exclusive prefix sum offsets: offset[0x02] = 0, offset[0x1A] = 2, offset[0xFF] = 3.
   - Stable scatter left-to-right into scratch buffer: [0x0302, 0x0102, 0x031A, 0x01FF].

2. **Pass 1 (High byte, shift = 8, mask = 0xFF)**:
   - Extract high bytes from scratch buffer: 0x03, 0x01, 0x03, 0x01.
   - Histogram counts: count[0x01] = 2, count[0x03] = 2.
   - Exclusive prefix sum offsets: offset[0x01] = 0, offset[0x03] = 2.
   - Stable scatter back to input buffer: [0x0102, 0x01FF, 0x0302, 0x031A].

Notice how stability on Pass 1 preserved the relative order of 0x0102 before 0x01FF (both high byte 0x01) and 0x0302 before 0x031A (both high byte 0x03).

sections.content:
## Hardware & cache mechanics

Modern CPUs spend up to 15–20 cycles recovering from a branch misprediction. In Quicksort, partitioning around a median compares unpredictable keys, causing ~50% branch misprediction rates on random inputs until branchless CMOV optimizations are applied. Radix Sort has zero key-comparison branches.

Its bottleneck shifts entirely to L1d cache capacity and store-buffer/TLB pressure during the scatter phase. With r = 8 bits (256 buckets * 4-byte uint32 counts = 1 KB), the histogram fits comfortably inside a 32 KB or 48 KB L1d cache alongside loop variables. Furthermore, fusing histogram computation for *all* d passes into a single pre-scan of the input array eliminates half of the read traffic—a standard optimization in Ska Sort and IPS4o-style hybrids.

## Algorithmic comparison

| Algorithm | Time Complexity | Extra Space | Branch Mispredicts | Stability | Best Fit |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Counting Sort** | O(n + k) | O(n + k) | Zero | Stable | Dense small integers (k <= 4n) |
| **LSD Radix Sort (r=8)** | O(d(n + 256)) | O(n + 256) | Zero | Stable | 32/64-bit ints, floats, fixed keys |
| **MSD Radix Sort (American Flag)** | O(d * n) avg | O(256 * depth) | Low | Unstable (in-place) | Variable-length strings, early exit |
| **Introsort (std::sort)** | O(n log n) | O(log n) | High on random | Unstable | General comparators, small n |
| **Timsort** | O(n log n) | O(n) | Medium | Stable | Partially ordered object arrays |

## Failure modes

1. **L1/TLB thrashing from oversized radix**: Picking r = 16 (65,536 buckets) creates a 256 KB histogram and scatters across 65,536 distinct streams, overflowing the 64-entry L1 DTLB.
2. **Signed & IEEE-754 ordering bugs**: Negative two's-complement integers have MSB = 1, and negative IEEE-754 floats are stored in sign-magnitude order (more negative = larger bit pattern). Failing to apply the order-preserving bijection scrambles negative values.
3. **Degenerate MSD recursion**: Deeply shared prefixes in MSD Radix Sort without a small-bucket cutoff (e.g., n <= 16 -> Insertion Sort) waste stack frames and zeroing cycles on 1-element buckets.
4. **Memory bandwidth saturation on small n**: For n < 1,000, allocating a scratch buffer and clearing 256-entry histograms costs more than an in-cache Insertion Sort or Quicksort.

## Production adoption & hybrids

Production systems rarely use textbook Counting Sort in isolation; they use cache-aware hybrids:
- **Rust `radsort` / C++ `ska_sort`**: Pre-compute all d histograms in a single pass, skip any digit pass where all keys share the same byte value (histogram[v] == n), and fall back to Insertion Sort on small MSD partitions.
- **GPU Radix Sort (NVIDIA CUB `DeviceRadixSort`)**: Uses 4-bit or 8-bit digits with warp-level shared-memory histograms and decoupled look-back prefix sums to sort >10 billion 32-bit keys/sec on H100 GPUs.
- **DuckDB & ClickHouse**: Combine 8-bit MSD Radix Sort with normalized binary sort keys (encoding NULL flags, descending order via bitwise NOT, and fixed-prefix string bytes) so multi-column SQL `ORDER BY` executes as a pure byte-wise radix sort.

## Practical checklist

- [ ] Verify keys can be bijected into fixed-width unsigned integers or lexicographic byte strings.
- [ ] Apply sign-bit XOR for signed integers and conditional bit-flip for IEEE-754 floats before pass 0, then invert on completion.
- [ ] Use r = 8 bits (256 buckets) as the default radix to guarantee L1d cache residency.
- [ ] Pre-compute all d pass histograms in one initial scan and skip passes where a single bucket holds all n elements.
- [ ] Fall back to Insertion Sort or Introsort when n < 64 (or when MSD bucket size drops below 16).
- [ ] Benchmark against `std::sort` / `slices.Sort` on both uniform random and skewed/pre-sorted distributions.

interviewProblems.title: Counting & Radix Sort
interviewProblems.scenarioPrompt: Design a production system that depends on Counting & Radix Sort. What invariants, failure modes, and observability do you require?
interviewProblems.sampleDefense: Start from invariants, choose the pattern that preserves them, and add metrics for the known failure modes.
commonPitfalls: Optimizing throughput before defining correctness boundaries.

nodes.label: Ping-Pong Output Buffer
nodes.role: Swaps role with input each pass

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: Counting and Radix Sort bypass the Ω(n log n) comparison lower bound by indexing keys directly into frequency buckets or sorting digit-by-digit in O(n + k) or O(d(n + b)) time.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: Stable Scatter Unit applies the primary invariant and coordinates with Ping-Pong Output Buffer.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, Ping-Pong Output Buffer experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Cap radix at 8 bits (256 buckets, 1–2 KB) or 11 bits (2,048 buckets, 8–16 KB) so the entire histogram stays resident in L1d.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: When keys are bounded integers, fixed-width strings, or IEEE-754 floats, non-comparative distribution sorting outperforms Quicksort and Timsort by eliminating branch mispredictions and log-factor passes.
Avoid trap: Using unstable Counting Sort inside an LSD Radix Sort loop, which destroys the ordering established by lower-significance digits.
Avoid trap: Forgetting to zero-initialize the histogram array between radix passes, corrupting prefix-sum offsets.
When to reach for it: Sorting large arrays (n > 10,000) of fixed-width integers, timestamps, IPv4/IPv6 addresses, or IEEE-754 floats where key bit-width is small (32–128 bits).
When to reach for it: Building high-throughput database operators (hash-join partitioning, columnar dictionary encoding, LSM-tree SSTable compaction) where branch-free throughput matters.

putItTogether.title: Putting Counting Radix Sort Together
putItTogether.summary: When keys are bounded integers, fixed-width strings, or IEEE-754 floats, non-comparative distribution sorting outperforms Quicksort and Timsort by eliminating branch mispredictions and log-factor passes.
steps: Establish baseline invariants for Counting Radix Sort before scaling.
Isolate hot paths with caching, backpressure, or partitioning.
Verify failure modes with synthetic load & chaos checks.
putItTogether.outcome: An 8-pass LSD Radix Sort (8-bit radix, 256-entry L1-resident histogram) completes in ~420 ms on a single core with zero branch mispredictions, versus ~2.8 s for std::sort (Introsort), achieving a 6.6x speedup.
